metadata.title: Trump moves to replace Texas judicial nominee opposed by Senator Cornyn

sources.news_title: Trump Moves to Replace Texas Judicial Nominee Opposed by Sen. Cornyn
Spurned GOP senator gets his revenge as Trump forced into embarrassing judicial retreat
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is backing away from one of his judicial nominees in Texas after Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, blocked the pick in one of his final acts in office.
Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-IA) said late Wednesday that his committee had received partial nomination paperwork for Steve Fahey, a former prosecutor Cornyn supports for a federal judgeship in Dallas, Reuters reported.
Trump had originally chosen T. Elliot Gaiser for the seat, but last week Cornyn refused to return a "blue slip" for Gaiser. Under longstanding Senate custom, that move effectively stops a trial court nominee from advancing, and the outgoing senator did not hold back about his reasons.
Cornyn said Gaiser was not even from Texas and that the White House "was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate vetting for a lifetime job."
Gaiser is a former Ohio solicitor general who clerked for Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito and now leads the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, the unit that has often signed off on the legality of the Trump administration's actions. He had the support of Texas' other Republican senator, Ted Cruz.
The setback comes as the White House rushes to confirm as many judges as possible before Democrats take over the Senate on Jan. 3 with a 56-seat majority after their sweeping midterm wins.
Cornyn's objection is the latest in a series of GOP senators opposing judicial picks from their own states, and the White House has already had to replace one nominee to whom his home-state Republican senators objected.
Grassley's office said he would consult his colleagues to determine whether Fahey and another newly announced nominee, Jim O'Neill of North Carolina, have "viable paths to confirmation." With just weeks left before the handover, that is far from certain.
The White House did not respond to Reuters' request for comment.
Over his two terms, Trump has appointed 295 judges to lifetime positions, including three of the six conservative justices on the Supreme Court.

sources.news_title: Humiliated Trump forced to swap judge pick after Texas GOP revolt
sources.text:
After a Republican senator put a roadblock in the way of his federal judicial nominee, President Donald Trump has officially caved and switched to a new nominee.
On Wednesday evening, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said that his committee had received a partial nomination package for Steve Fahey, a former prosecutor, to fill a vacancy on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas based in Dallas, the Independent reported. Fahey's nomination is for a position Trump had initially offered to Justice Department official T. Elliot Gaiser.
The change represents a victory for outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who supported Fahey's nomination and refused last week to return his "blue slip" for Gaiser. The "blue slip" is a Senate tradition that allows senators to veto the nomination of a district court judge in their state.
Sources close to Cornyn said this week that Gaiser was a "dead" nominee, and the senator had publicly called on Trump to nominate Fahey instead. He had said that Gaiser is not even from Texas and that the White House was attempting to "jam him down our throat without adequate vetting for a lifetime job."
Gaiser is a former Ohio solicitor general who clerked for Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. He is currently heading the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, which has frequently provided legal cover for the administration's actions. Gaiser was nominated after the election by Trump with the support of Texas' other Republican senator, Ted Cruz.
Cornyn is the latest Republican senator to block his own state's judicial nominee, and this is the second time the White House has had to switch nominees after home-state Republican senators objected.
Cornyn doesn't owe Trump anything. Trump endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton against Cornyn in the primary, and Cornyn lost. The seat ended up going to Democrat James Talarico in November.
Trump allies had expected Cornyn to buckle and not risk allowing Democrats to fill the position, according to MS NOW. Instead, the White House caved.
The standoff comes at a time when the administration is racing to fill lifetime judgeships before Democrats take control of the Senate on Jan. 3, when they will hold a 56-seat majority. Trump has installed 295 lifetime judges during his two terms, including three justices on the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority.
Still, Fahey's nomination is not guaranteed to go through. Grassley's office said that he will consult with other senators about whether he thinks Fahey's nomination, along with that of Jim O'Neill, a new nominee from North Carolina, can be confirmed.

Steve Fahey, a former prosecutor, is in line for a Dallas-based federal judgeship after President Donald Trump moved to replace one of his Texas judicial nominees.
Chuck Grassley, the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, said late Wednesday that his panel had received partial nomination paperwork for Fahey, backed by outgoing Republican senator John Cornyn. Trump had previously nominated T. Elliot Gaiser, a Justice Department official, for that seat.
Cornyn last week withheld a so-called blue slip backing Gaiser, preventing the original pick from advancing. The move marked the latest instance of a Republican senator opposing a judicial nominee in the lawmaker's home state.
Cornyn, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, objected to Gaiser, saying he was not even from Texas and that the White House "was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate vetting for a lifetime job."
The opposition has complicated White House efforts to confirm as many of Trump's remaining judicial nominees as possible before Democrats take control of the Senate in January.
Democrats assume Senate control on January 3 after winning a 56-seat majority in the recent election. The White House has already been forced to replace one nominee opposed by his state's Republican senators.
Grassley's office said the Iowa Republican would consult with his colleagues to determine whether Fahey and another newly announced nominee, North Carolina's Jim O'Neill, have viable paths to confirmation. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump nominated Gaiser to a seat on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election, with the support of Texas' other Republican senator, Ted Cruz. Gaiser, a former Ohio solicitor general, previously clerked for conservative U.S. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito.
He currently heads the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, a key unit that has frequently signed off on the legality of the Trump administration's actions. Under Senate custom, home-state senators play an influential role in selecting nominees for federal courts in their states.
They can effectively block trial court picks they oppose by refusing to return a blue slip signaling support. Across his two terms, Trump has secured 295 judicial nominees to lifetime positions. Those appointments include three members of the U.S. Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority.
